extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP litigators, patent agents, and law students studying U.S. obviousness law
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether a claimed invention is obvious under 35 U.S.C. §103 in light of prior art and case law (especially KSR v. Teleflex), including factual inquiries and legal conclusions used in litigation and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory obviousness standard (35 U.S.C. §103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness under §103: patentability is precluded when the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition is the starting point for analysis. Interpretations and applications are shaped by Graham and later cases; treat it as the legal standard to be applied through subsidiary factual inquiries (scope/content of prior art; differences with claims; level of ordinary skill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Graham, determine (1) the scope and content of the prior art, (2) the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, and (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; then weigh secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this roadmap to structure the obviousness inquiry. Secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, etc.) may be used to illuminate the circumstances surrounding invention and to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what the prior art discloses (including references not in the exact field if they are analogous) and the teachings it contains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both explicit teachings and what can be inferred by a person of ordinary skill; analogous-art analysis matters but the court may consider cross-field references when they address the same need or problem (KSR; In re Icon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between claims and prior art (claim scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertain claim scope and what features differ from the prior art; claim scope is a question of law informed by claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad claim scope may make combining prior art more likely to render claims obvious; avoid reading unclaimed limitations into claims to escape relevant prior art (district court guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the attributes and knowledge of a person having ordinary skill in the pertinent art, recognizing that such a person has ordinary creativity and is not an automaton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the skill level carefully because it affects what combinations, inferences, and routine adaptations would have been obvious; consider educational background, practical experience, and what problems and solutions were common knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine prior art (TSM as a factor, not rigid rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill to combine elements of the prior art in the way claimed; KSR rejected TSM as a rigid test but acknowledged motive can inform analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation may be explicit in prior art or implicit in market forces, design incentives, known benefits, or common sense; courts require some articulated reasoning but not necessarily precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter (Translogic; Aventis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of results
rubrics_metrics.description: If the combination of known elements does no more than yield predictable results according to their established functions, the combination is likely obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the improvement is more than the predictable use of prior-art elements. Courts use predictability as a key touchstone (KSR, Great Atlantic). Examples: updating mechanical devices with modern electronics often yields predictable results (Leapfrog).

rubrics_metrics.name: Synergy / unexpected cooperative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination that produces an effect greater than the sum of the parts (unexpected, fruitful synergy) supports nonobviousness; combinations that merely arrange old elements each performing the same function are more likely obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anderson’s-Black Rock and Sakraida emphasize synergy; KSR resurrected those concerns but did not require synergy as a rigid rule. Synergy is strong evidence of nonobviousness when present (Adams contrasted as example of unexpected interaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior art teaches away from the claimed combination (suggests that the combination would not work or should not be tried), that evidence favors nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat teaching away as weighty evidence of nonobviousness (Adams). Conversely, absence of such teaching or prior art that points unmistakably toward the combination supports obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" and finite predictable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a design need or market pressure exists and there are a finite number of identified predictable solutions, it may have been obvious to try known options and, if success was predictable, the result may be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: in some technologies (e.g., chemistry), 'obvious to try' requires a reasonable expectation of success and identification of a motivation to try a particular modification; known risks or negative side effects can negate 'obvious to try' (Takeda).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia / secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider objective evidence of nonobviousness such as commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, unexpected results, and other indicia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations can rebut a prima facie showing of obviousness and should be evaluated in context; courts have found them insufficient in some cases where predictability or prior teachings were strong (Friskit, Leapfrog).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense and common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges may rely on common sense and the general creative capacity of a PHOSITA to supply inferences about what combinations would have been obvious, without rigid formalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR endorses a flexible, common-sense approach; courts may take account of inferences and creative steps a PHOSITA would employ rather than requiring precise textual teachings in prior art (Translogic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art / cross-field references
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art need not be limited to the exact field of endeavor if references from another field address the same need or problem and would have motivated PHOSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Icon and other cases show courts will consider references from different fields when the problem and solution are analogous; district courts examine whether references are analogous and whether a motive to combine exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for articulated reasoning / rational underpinning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts require some articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning to support a legal conclusion of obviousness, even if exact teachings are not present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While KSR allows implicit motivation and common-sense inferences, courts still expect a reasoned explanation (Aventis). Boilerplate assertions without reasoning are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operability and inoperability evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the claimed combination would be inoperable or uniquely difficult to make may weigh against a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will consider whether PHOSITA would have known how to make the combination operable; claim breadth can affect this analysis. Lack of evidence of difficulty may support obviousness (Icon; Leapfrog observation about reduction-to-practice difficulty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for summary judgment on obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is ultimately a legal determination; summary judgment is appropriate when the prior art, claim scope, and level of ordinary skill are not in material dispute and obviousness is apparent from those factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the key factual predicates are undisputed and the obviousness conclusion follows as a matter of law, courts may grant summary judgment (KSR). However, genuine disputes of material fact (e.g., analogous art, motive to combine, secondary considerations) preclude summary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-specific considerations (chemicals, compounds, biotech)
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain fields (especially chemical compounds), it remains necessary to identify a reason a chemist would have modified known compounds in a particular manner to establish prima facie obviousness; unpredictable results or known negatives may defeat 'obvious to try'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Takeda and Aventis show that in chemistry courts require more concrete reasons to combine or modify compounds. Treat 'obvious to try' more stringently in such fields and present evidence about expectations of success and side effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial / market forces as motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design incentives, market pressure, or commonly understood benefits (e.g., reduced size, lower cost, increased reliability, increased marketability) can supply a rationale to combine prior art elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts recognize market incentives as legitimate reasons a PHOSITA would pursue known options; point to market-driven motivations when defending obviousness, and consider whether those incentives would have made success predictable (Leapfrog; Translogic).
